result:
A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the unpredictable timing of two or more processes touching the same resource. With a shared log, two scripts can write at the same moment and leave interleaved or lost lines.

To avoid it, always append with `>>` (never `>`) and take an exclusive lock around each entry with `flock`:

```sh
LOG=/var/log/shared.log

(
  flock 9
  printf '%s %s\n' "$(date -Is)" "$msg" >&9
) 9>>"$LOG"
```

The `9>>"$LOG"` opens the log in append mode on file descriptor 9, `flock 9` blocks until this process holds the lock, and the lock is released when the subshell exits.

`flock` is advisory, so it only protects you if every writer to that file uses the same pattern. It is also unreliable on some network filesystems such as NFS; there, have each process write its own file or send entries to `logger`/syslog instead.

For single short lines on a local filesystem, a bare `>>` is usually safe on its own, because each append is written at the end of the file in one step. The lock matters once an entry spans multiple lines or multiple commands.
